L29@P1: Human eosinophils express the eotaxin receptor, CCR3, but
L30@P1: respond to a variety of CC chemokines apart from eotaxin,
L31@P1: including RANTES, monocyte chemotactic protein (MCP)-2,
L32@P1: MCP-3, and MCP-4. Here we describe a mAb, 7B11, that is
L33@P1: selective for CCR3 and has the properties of a true receptor
L34@P1: antagonist. 7B11 blocked binding of various radiolabeled
L35@P1: chemokines to either CCR3 transfectants, or eosinophils.
L36@P1: Pretreatment of eosinophils with this mAb blocked chemotaxis and calcium flux induced by all CCR3 ligands. In all
L37@P1: individuals examined, including allergic and eosinophilic
L38@P1: donors, . 95% of the response of eosinophils to eotaxin,
L39@P1: RANTES, MCP-2, MCP-3, and MCP-4 was shown to be
L40@P1: mediated through CCR3. The IL-8 receptors, particularly
L41@P1: CXCR2, were induced on IL-5 primed eosinophils, however
L42@P1: these eosinophils responded to CC chemokines in the same
L43@P1: manner as unprimed eosinophils. These results demonstrate
L44@P1: the importance of CCR3 for eosinophil responses, and the
L45@P1: feasibility of completely antagonizing this receptor. (J. Clin. Invest. 1997. 99:178–184.) Key words: chemokines • eosinophils •
L46@P1: receptors-cytokine • cell movement • eotaxin
L47@P1: Introduction
L48@P1: Chemokines mediate a range of pro-inflammatory effects on
L49@P1: leukocytes, including chemotaxis, degranulation, and integrin
L50@P1: activation (1, 2). Numerous chemokines have been identified,
L51@P1: and all bind to seven transmembrane spanning G-protein coupled receptors (7TMR*) (3–5). The best characterized chemokine receptors are the IL-8 receptor A (now termed CXCR1)
L52@P1: which binds IL-8, and the IL-8 receptor B (CXCR2) which
L53@P1: binds a number of the CXC or a chemokines, including IL-8
L54@P1: and GROa (3, 5). The known receptors for the CC or b
L55@P1: chemokines include CCR1, which binds macrophage inflammatory protein (MIP)-1a,
L56@P1: 1
L57@P1:  RANTES and MCP-3 (4, 6–8),
L58@P1: CCR2, which binds MCP-1 and MCP-3 (8, 9), CCR3, which
L59@P1: binds eotaxin, RANTES and MCP-3 (10), CCR4 which binds
L60@P1: MCP-1, MIP-1a, and RANTES (11, 12), and CCR5 which
L61@P1: binds MIP-1a, MIP-1b, and RANTES (13–15). The expression
L62@P1: of these receptors on different leukocyte subsets influences
L63@P1: their migration to inflammatory sites. Neutrophils respond to
L64@P1: many of the CXC chemokines (1), whereas T cells respond to
L65@P1: the CC chemokines MCP-1, MCP-3, RANTES, MIP-1a, and
L66@P1: MIP-1b (16–18), and the CXC chemokines IP-10, Mig, and
L67@P1: SDF-1 (reviewed in reference 19).
L68@P1: Chemokine receptor usage by eosinophils has generated
L69@P1: considerable interest, because eosinophils are selectively recruited to certain inflammatory sites (20, 21), and receptor antagonists may be useful for blocking eosinophil entry and degranulation in diseases such as asthma.Many chemokines have
L70@P1: been reported to act on human eosinophils; RANTES, MCP-2,
L71@P1: and MCP-3 were the first chemokines to be identified as eosinophil chemoattractants (22–24), followed recently by eotaxin
L72@P1: (25) and MCP-4 (26). MIP-1a was found to be a weak chemoattractant in some studies (10, 23, 27), while IL-8 was found to attract eosinophils only after IL-5 stimulation (28). This array of
L73@P1: ligands suggested a complex pattern of receptor expression on
L74@P1: eosinophils. CCR1, the MIP-1a/RANTES receptor, was considered as a possible receptor on eosinophils for CC chemokines, but [Ca21]i
L75@P1:  desensitization and ligand binding studies
L76@P1: implicated the existence of a distinct eosinophil receptor (22,
L77@P1: 25, 29). CCR3, the eotaxin receptor, has subsequently been
L78@P1: identified as a major CC chemokine receptor on eosinophils
L79@P1: (10, 30). When transfected into a murine pre B lymphoma line,
L80@P1: CCR3 bound eotaxin, RANTES and MCP-3, but not MIP-1a,
L81@P1: and conferred chemotactic responses on these cells to eotaxin,
L82@P1: RANTES and MCP-3 (10). The role of CCR1, CCR2, CCR4
L83@P1: and CCR5 on eosinophils is still unresolved, as is the receptor(s) on eosinophils used by MCP-2 and MCP-4.
L84@P1: Because of the complicated pattern of receptor binding and
L85@P1: signaling by the chemokines, it has been difficult to determine
L86@P1: the significance of a particular receptor on a given leukocyte
L87@P1: type. In addition, Northern blot or ligand binding are sometimes not sensitive enough for detecting expression of chemokine receptors, which can be expressed at , 1,000 sites per cell
L88@P1: (31). One way to address this is to develop specific receptor
L89@P1: antagonists. Here we report on the first fully antagonistic mAb
L90@P1: for a CC chemokine receptor. Anti-CCR3 mAb 7B11 completely blocks the binding and signaling of the known ligands

L97@P2: for CCR3. We show that human eosinophils use CCR3 and
L98@P2: not other CC chemokine receptors, for their responses to eotaxin, RANTES, MCP-2, MCP-3 and MCP-4. Eosinophils activated in vitro with IL-5 showed the same properties, but upregulated CXCR1 and CXCR2.
L99@P2: Methods
L100@P2: Cells, cell lines, and tissue culture. Eosinophils were isolated from heparinized blood using CD16 microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec, Auburn,
L101@P2: CA), as described (25) and were shown cytologically to be 99% pure.
L102@P2: Neutrophils and PBMCs were isolated as described (25). To generate
L103@P2: CD3 blasts, 2 3 106 PBMC/ml in RPMI-1640 plus 10% FCS were
L104@P2: added to tissue culture plates first coated with the anti-CD3 antibody
L105@P2: TR66. After 4–6 d blasts were removed to fresh media and supplemented with IL-2 (kindly provided by Antonio Lanzavecchia, Basel,
L106@P2: Switzerland) at 50 U/ml. Other cell lines used included transfectants
L107@P2: of the L1.2 murine pre B cell lymphoma, expressing high levels of either CCR3 (10), IL-8 RA (10), IL-8 RB (10), CCR2b (G. LaRosa,
L108@P2: manuscript in preparation), CCR4 and CCR5 (Lijun Wu, manuscript
L109@P2: in preparation), and CCR1 (32). Transfectants were maintained in
L110@P2: RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% bovine serum and 800 mg/ml
L111@P2: G418. The different transfectants were monitored for expression of
L112@P2: the relevant receptors, using mAbs specific for CCR3 (10), IL-8 RA,
L113@P2: IL-8 RB, or CCR2 (16, 25). For CCR4 and CCR5, expression was
L114@P2: monitored using the anti-flag mAb M2, since these receptors were
L115@P2: constructed with this epitope at the NH2 terminus. Human eosinophils were cultured with 5 ng/ml of recombinant human IL-5 (Genzyme Corp., Cambridge, MA), for 5–7 d, using tissue culture flasks
L116@P2: containing sub confluent monolayers of ECV304 cells.
L117@P2: mAb production and flow cytometry. mAbs reactive with CCR3
L118@P2: were generated by immunizing C57BL6 mice with 107 L1.2 CCR3
L119@P2: transfected cells, intraperitoneally, five to six times at 2-wk intervals.
L120@P2: The final immunization was injected intravenously. 4 d later, the
L121@P2: spleen was removed and cells were fused with the SP2/0 cell line as
L122@P2: described (33). mAbs reactive with CCR3 were identified using untransfected and CCR3 transfected L1.2 cells, and immunofluorescent
L123@P2: staining and analysis using a FACScan® (Becton Dickinson & Co.,
L124@P2: Mountain View, CA). mAbs to IL-8 RA, IL-8 RB, and CCR2 (MCP1R) have been described (16). mAb staining of cells was performed
L125@P2: using standard procedures, as described previously (10). To enumerate antibody binding sites per cell, the following protocol was used:
L126@P2: 100 ml of whole blood from donors was reacted with a supersaturating
L127@P2: amount (400 ng) of a 7B11-FITC preparation in PBS with 0.5% azide
L128@P2: at room temperature. Red cells were lysed with ammonium chloride
L129@P2: lysing solution and the mean channel fluorescence of 7B11 stained
L130@P2: cells was determined by flow cytometry. At the same time, the number of MESF units per antibody molecule was determined by saturating the sites on Simply Cellular beads (Flow Cytometry Standards
L131@P2: Corp., San Juan, PR) with 7B11-FITC and reading the mean channel
L132@P2: fluorescence of the beads on the flow cytometer. The flow cytometer
L133@P2: was calibrated to equate mean channel numbers with MESF units using Quantum 26 beads (Flow Cytometry Standards Corp.). The number of antibody molecules per cell could then be calculated by calculating the MESF equivalents of the mean channel fluorescence of the
L134@P2: cells and dividing by the MESF units per antibody molecule.
L135@P2: Chemokines, chemotaxis assays, and ligand-binding assay. Recombinant human chemokines were obtained from Peprotech (Rocky Hill,
L136@P2: NJ), except for eotaxin, described previously (25), which was a gift of
L137@P2: Dr. Ian Clark-Lewis. Chemotaxis of human eosinophils was assessed
L138@P2: using a modification of a transendothelial assay (17), using the cell
L139@P2: line ECV304 exactly as described (25). Cells that had migrated to the
L140@P2: bottom chamber were placed in a tube, and relative cell counts were
L141@P2: obtained using the FACScan®.
L142@P2: 125I-labeled eotaxin was obtained from Amersham Corp. (Arlington Heights, IL), and its specific activity was stated to be 2,000 Ci/
L143@P2: mM. Chemokine binding to target cells was carried out as described
L144@P2: previously (25, 34). Cells were washed once in PBS and resuspended
L145@P2: in binding buffer (50 mM Hepes, pH 7.5, 1 mM CaCl, 5 mM MgCl2,
L146@P2: 0.5% BSA, and 0.05% azide) at a concentration of 107/ml. Aliquots of
L147@P2: 50 ml (5 3 105 cells) were dispensed into microfuge tubes, followed by
L148@P2: the addition of cold competitor and radiolabeled chemokines as indicated in the text. The final reaction volume was 200 ml. After a 60-
L149@P2: min incubation at room temperature, the cells were washed three
L150@P2: times with 1 ml of binding buffer containing 0.5 M NaCl. Cell pellets
L151@P2: were then counted. The competition was presented as the percent
L152@P2: specific binding as calculated by 100 3 [(S2B)/(T2B)], where S is the
L153@P2: radioactivity of the sample, B is background binding, and T is total
L154@P2: binding without competitors. Background binding was obtained by
L155@P2: incubating cells with radiolabeled chemokine and at least 400-fold excess of unlabeled chemokines. Duplicates were used throughout the
L156@P2: experiments and the standard deviations were always , 10% of the
L157@P2: mean. All experiments were repeated at least three times. Curve fit
L158@P2: and concentrations that inhibit 50% specific binding (IC50) were calculated by KaleidaGraph software (Synergy Software, Reading, PA).

L289@P4: Discussion
L290@P4: Here we showed that the functional effects of all of the efficacious chemokines for eosinophils-eotaxin, RANTES, MCP-2,
L291@P4: MCP-3, or MCP-4, could be blocked completely with an antiCCR3 mAb. This mAb was specific for CCR3, and had no inhibitory effects on other chemoattractant receptors. These results establish that CCR3 is indeed the principal receptor for
L292@P4: eosinophil responses to CC chemokines, and questions an essential role for CCR1, CCR2, CCR4, or CCR5. These results
L293@P4: also establish that the development of potent antagonists for
L294@P4: the chemokine receptor family is viable, at least by the mAb
L295@P4: approach.
L296@P4: CCR3 is expressed selectively and at high levels on eosinophils, as shown by ligand binding studies (10), and also staining
L297@P4: with mAb 7B11. We also find expression of CCR3 on basophils and some T cell clones as well as tissue macrophages (unpublished observation). Before the identification of CCR3,
L298@P4: there was indirect evidence for the expression of a MIP-1a/
L299@P4: RANTES receptor on eosinophils, as well as a receptor with
L300@P4: properties consistent with those of CCR3 (29). Also, a recent
L301@P4: study suggested that human eosinophils express MIP-1a receptors, either CCR1, CCR4 or CCR5, at about 1–5% of the
L302@P4: levels of CCR3 (27). We have been able to demonstrate modest eosinophil chemotactic responses towards MIP-1a in some
L303@P4: individuals (10, 25), nevertheless our results show that a MIP-1a
L304@P4: receptor contributes little to the functional responses of eosinophils to the major eosinophilic chemoattractants: RANTES,
L305@P4: MCP-3 or MCP-4. We have observed donor to donor variation
L306@P4: in eosinophil responses to the CC chemokines, however we
L307@P4: were able to block these responses completely in all individuals, using mAb 7B11, suggesting that if other CC chemokine
L308@P4: receptors are present, they have a minor functional significance. It is conceivable that inhibition of CCR3 somehow
L309@P4: cross-inhibits the functions of other CC chemokine receptors,
